name: Plaster of Paris (set gypsum, casting grade)
summary: Gypsum rock heated until it gives up three quarters of its water becomes calcium sulfate hemihydrate. Mixed with water it recrystallises within minutes into an interlocking mass of gypsum needles, expanding very slightly, which is why it takes the finest detail of a mould. The water beyond the small amount the reaction needs leaves as pores, so a set cast is about half void, soft, absorbent and slightly soluble. It is the substance of the four casts in the Rotunda's niches and of the face of every fibrous plaster piece.

formation.how: Gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) is calcined to the hemihydrate (CaSO4·½H2O), ground fine and sold as casting or moulding plaster. Strewn into water and mixed, it sets by recrystallising to gypsum. The water-to-plaster ratio governs the density and strength of the cast.

specularF0.derivation: normal-incidence Fresnel reflectance R0 = ((n-1)/(n+1))^2 over gypsum's alpha (1.521) and gamma (1.530) indices

naturalGroundGypsum.derivation: Y/Yn = (L/100)^2 from Hunter L = 88.0 (HunterLab Colorflex EZ); a = 0.8, b = 4.3 show a faint warm cast
naturalGroundGypsum.note: ground natural white gypsum filler (98 % CaSO4·2H2O, median particle size 13.0 um in the property table, though the same sheet's Microtrac table puts 50 % finer than 22 um); impurities in natural rock hold it below the whitest calcined plasters. The sheet prints 'L, a, b values (3) 88.0, 0.8, 4.3' with footnote 'HunterLab Colorflex EZ Colorimeter L,a,b values': unstarred, i.e. Hunter Lab notation, but the scale is not named; read as CIE L* = 88.0 the same reading would give Y/Yn = 0.72
naturalGroundGypsum.source: USG IG574-USA-ENG rev. 1-21, USG Terra Alba No. 1, https://www.usg.com/content/dam/USG/pdpmovedocuments/usg-terra-alba-no1-calcium-sulfate-filler-data-en-IG574.pdf; Hunter L = 100·sqrt(Y/Yn): Hunter, R.S. & Harold, R.W. (1987) The Measurement of Appearance, 2nd ed., Wiley, formula as given at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter_Lab

reflectanceStandardUse.text: Plaster of Paris set in water (1:3 by mass) was studied as a field diffuse-reflectance standard for its high reflectance, fairly flat spectrum and nearly perfect diffuseness.
reflectanceStandardUse.source: Arai, T. (1979) Gypsum as Reflectance Standard in Field Works. Transactions of the Society of Instrument and Control Engineers 15(5), 678-682, https://doi.org/10.9746/sicetr1965.15.678 (abstract)

optics.wet: Set plaster is about half open pore; water filling the pores lowers the index contrast at crystal boundaries and the cast darkens and loses its chalky scatter until it dries.

porosity.source: USG IG1375 rev. 8-24 (dry density) and Handbook of Mineralogy: Gypsum (grain density), http://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/gypsum.pdf

hardness.note: varies with direction; a fingernail scratches it

solubility25c.note: spread of published estimates; 2.5-3.1 g of CaSO4·2H2O per litre
solubility25c.source: Lebedev, A.L. & Kosorukov, V.L. (2017) Gypsum solubility in water at 25 °C. Geochemistry International 55(2), 205-210, https://doi.org/10.1134/S0016702917010062

acoustic.note: Casts are free-standing objects in niches; their absorption belongs to the niche surface. Fibrous plaster panels carry their own record.

physicalMaterial.note: Not walked on and not to be touched: the casts stand in niches above the floor. No footfall class.

pieceMouldSections.text: Large figures are cast in separate moulds (head, limbs, torso); limbs are cast around iron rods; the portions are joined with steel dowels and fresh plaster, and the joins are sealed with plaster and paint or left detachable.

finePlasterLining.text: Only superfine plaster is used for small casts or for lining the moulds of large ones; a thin skin of fine plaster over coarser plaster chips off in transport.
finePlasterLining.source: Brigham, W.T. (1874), pp. 27-29, as quoted in Payne, E.M. (2020) Studies in Conservation 65(1), 37-58, https://doi.org/10.1080/00393630.2019.1610845

photograph: A network of fine raised seam lines where the pieces of the mould met; fine sharp lines mean a good mould, thick ridges a worn one.
A matt, chalky, faintly warm white, or a tinted and waxed coat: nineteenth-century casts were often sealed, tinted with earth pigments or waxed.
Sub-millimetre pinholes from air trapped against the mould face.
Thick grey dust on upward-facing forms (heads, shoulders, the tops of drapery folds); on old casts, corroding iron armatures inside slender parts.
Old repairs: rejoined slender parts, fills and paint that read slightly differently from the original skin.

evidenceSearch.tier: The local sets are reference photographs of unknown exposure (texture, relief and ageing pattern only). Albedo needs tier (b), a ColorChecker photograph of a physical specimen; tier (a) here gives only the bounds listed under optics.luminousReflectance.

unverified.field: luminous reflectance of a clean, uncoated cast of high-purity casting plaster
unverified.reason: No measured value for a set cast was found. Ground natural gypsum measures 0.77 (derived from Hunter L); calcined high-purity casting plaster is whiter than natural rock, and Arai (1979) used set plaster as a reflectance standard for its high reflectance, but gives no number in the abstract. The tier (b) specimen sheet must settle it.

unverified.field: light transport depth (subsurface diffusion) in set plaster
unverified.reason: No measured scattering or absorption coefficient for set plaster was found; it governs how soft a cast's arrises look.

unverified.field: seam line width and height on a piece-mould cast
unverified.reason: Sources describe them as fine raised lines that thicken with mould wear, without numbers.
